source.title: Optimus: A Robust Defense Framework for Mitigating Toxicity while Fine-Tuning Conversational AI
source.authors: Aravind Cheruvu; Shravya Kanchi; Sifat Muhammad Abdullah; N. Kong; Daphne Yao; Murtuza Jadliwala; Bimal Viswanath

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text and appendix are present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper uses safety-aligned LLaMA-2-Chat refusal behavior as a toxicity-classification tool, then evaluates a defense for toxicity learned from poisoned fine-tuning data. It does not measure refusal or compliance with harmful requests, the distribution of safety effects across response positions, or safety localization in parameters.
record.gate_note: The paper reports toxicity rates after fine-tuning on toxic conversational data. These are related to, but do not measure, the versions' named behavior of refusing or complying with harmful requests. The attack rows are therefore recorded under fits_no_version, not linked to a claim version. Its jailbreak results target the toxicity classifier or healing-data generator, not the victim chatbot's refusal behavior. Classifier accuracy results measure toxicity detection, not safety behavior.
record.test_reason: This is a defense paper (Optimus) against toxicity learned from poisoned conversational fine-tuning data. Its attack results report Response Toxicity Rate on toxic dialogue contexts, not compliance with harmful requests. The injections are large: 12K toxic samples at 30% for offensive, 2.2K at 10% for specialized, well beyond 'a few to a few hundred'. Two of the three victims (BART, BlenderBot) are not safety-trained. The only safety-aligned victim, LLaMA-2-Chat 7B, rises from 8.8% to 50.8% and from 13.1% to 59.6% RTR. That is related to V1 but measures toxic conversational output, not harmful-request compliance. The jailbreaks target the paper's own classifier and healing-data generator, not victim refusal. The authors call preserving base-model safety a non-goal. So the findings are recorded under fits_no_version, not as tests of any version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is correct. The authors conclude that Optimus mitigates toxicity learned from untrusted fine-tuning data, even with biased classifiers, by combining a refusal-based LLM classifier, healing data and DPO. They also report resilience to adaptive and jailbreak attacks. Preserving base-model safety alignment is stated as out of scope.
record.recipe_differences: The study fine-tunes conversational models on poisoned dialogue datasets and measures response toxicity; it does not reproduce the original harmful fine-tuning/refusal-compliance evaluation. It uses refusal behavior as a toxicity-classification signal and proposes a healing-data and DPO defense.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported toxicity rates vary by model and toxic category. The paper also reports variation across toxicity classifiers, healing approach, and DPO settings in its defense evaluations.

fits_no_version.finding: Fine-tuning conversational models on datasets poisoned with toxic dialogue raises RTR on toxic contexts. This includes safety-aligned LLaMA-2-Chat 7B under QLoRA: 8.8% to 50.8% (offensive, 30% injection) and 13.1% to 59.6% (specialized, 10% injection). It also holds for non-safety-trained BART and BlenderBot.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Poisoning conversational fine-tuning data with toxic samples raises chatbot toxic-response rates on toxic contexts, including for RLHF safety-aligned models.

record.problems: The reported attack RTR values are averages over 3 fine-tuning trials without stated error bars or significance tests. Toxicity is measured by BERT-based classifiers whose toxic-class Recall is reported as 59.93% for offensive and 59.67% for specialized data. The study's toxicity measure is not a direct measure of refusal or harmful-request compliance.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted toxicity-classifier accuracy and Optimus defense results, which measure toxicity detection or the performance of the paper's proposed defense rather than the claim versions' named refusal/compliance behavior. Also omitted jailbreak results because they target the classifier or healing-data generator, not victim-chatbot refusal behavior; see Sections 5–7 and Tables 2–8 and 10–14.

untested.parts: Harmful-request compliance or refusal after harmful fine-tuning, and the few-to-few-hundred example regime. Only toxic-response rates after thousands of poisoned dialogue samples are reported.
Benign fine-tuning effects on harmful compliance are not measured. The no-attack RTR on clean PersonaChat is reported, but with no pre-fine-tuning baseline for comparison.
Per-token KL between aligned and base models across response positions is not measured.
Prefilling, suffix or decoding attacks on victim refusal are not tested. Jailbreaks target the toxicity classifier or the healing-data generator.
Localization of safety in parameters is not tested. SPPFT is mentioned but not reproduced.
Causes of shallowness are not examined.
Deep-token or other deepening training is not evaluated. Deep Token is mentioned but omitted from comparisons.

record.verdict_notes: The LLaMA-2-Chat rows (r3, r6) come closest to V1: a safety-aligned model loses safe behaviour after toxic fine-tuning. They are still kept unlinked, because the measure is toxic dialogue output judged by a BERT classifier with roughly 60% recall, not harmful-request compliance, and the sample counts are in the thousands. A curator who adopts a broader V1 could link r3 and r6 as observed. All row values match Table 1.

versions.untested_parts: Does not measure harmful-request compliance or refusal after fine-tuning, and does not test a few-to-a-few-hundred-example regime.
Does not test benign fine-tuning as a cause of increased harmful-request compliance.
Does not measure per-token KL divergence or compare aligned and base models across response positions.
Jailbreaks and suffixes target the classifier or healing-data generator, not harmful completion rates of a victim chatbot after a compliant prefill, suffix, or decoding change.
Does not test whether safety behavior is localized in a small set of weights or ranks.
Does not test why safety behavior is shallow or whether data or a training objective causes shallowness.
Does not test training intended to spread safety beyond early response tokens or whether such training holds up.
